title: Thanksgiving Parenting Time in Colorado: Tips for Co-Parents

content.rendered:
Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gratitude, good food, and maybe a nap during the football game. But if you’re divorced or separated, it can also come with a pressing and less festive question: Who has the kids this year?

This year, like all years, Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday in November, which is Thursday, November 26, 2026. If you and your co-parent haven’t talked about your Thanksgiving plan yet, now is the time, before the turkey is in the oven and tempers are running hot. Here are a few practical tips to help the day go smoothly for you and, most importantly, for your kids.

First, Pull Out Your Parenting Plan And Actually Read It

We know, it’s not exactly light and fluffy holiday reading. But your parenting plan is the rulebook, and most Colorado parenting plans include a holiday schedule that takes priority over your regular parenting time schedule. Look for:

  • Whose turn it is. Many plans alternate Thanksgiving, for example one parent in even years and the other in odd years.
  • When “Thanksgiving” starts and ends. Is it just Thursday? Wednesday after school through Sunday? Or after school on the Friday before Thanksgiving through the following Monday? Many Colorado school districts give kids the entire week off, so those details matter.
  • Exchange times and places. Does your plan set a specific time, or does it say “as agreed”?
  • Travel rules. Some plans require a 30 or 45 or 60-day notice of travel plans with an itinerary before a child travels out of state.

If it’s been a while since you looked at your holiday schedule, our guide to reviewing your holiday parenting plan early can help.

There’s More Than One Way to Share Thanksgiving

Colorado law doesn’t hand Thanksgiving to Mom or Dad. Courts approve whatever schedule is best for the children (C.R.S. § 14-10-124), and parents are free to agree on what works for their family. Some common setups:

  • Alternating years: one parent has the whole holiday this year, the other parent next year.
  • Dividing the day: turkey at one house, pie at the other. This works best when parents live close together (and when kids have room for two dinners).
  • Dividing the break: one parent has Wednesday through Thursday evening, the other has Friday through Sunday.
  • Same holiday every year: one parent always has Thanksgiving, the other always has a different holiday. This can work well for families with strong traditions.

Tips for a Calmer Thanksgiving

Confirm the plan now, in writing

Don’t wait until the Tuesday before. Send a short, friendly message confirming whose year it is, pickup and drop-off times, and where. A text, email, or co-parenting app works, and it gives you a record if questions come up later.

Have a backup plan for travel and weather

Thanksgiving week is one of the busiest travel times of the year, and Colorado weather loves a surprise. If your exchange involves I-70 or a flight, agree ahead of time on what happens if roads close or flights are delayed. Share flight details and where the kids will be staying.

Keep handoffs short and sweet

Holiday exchanges can be emotional for everyone. Keep them brief, polite, and focused on the kids. If there’s a scheduling disagreement, save it for later, away from little ears. These communication tips for co-parents can help.

Let the kids say hello to the other parent

A quick video call with the other parent on Thanksgiving Day can mean a lot to your children, and it costs you about five minutes. Unless your plan says otherwise, a little flexibility goes a long way.

Not your year? Start a new tradition

Thanksgiving doesn’t have to happen on Thursday. Plenty of families celebrate the weekend before or after with a “Friendsgiving,” a special breakfast, or a movie-and-leftovers day. Kids usually don’t complain about getting two celebrations.

Listen to your teens, but keep the grown-ups in charge

Teenagers have opinions (shocking, we know), plus friends, sports, and part-time jobs. Their input matters, but the parenting plan still controls. Try not to put them in the middle by asking them to pick where they’d rather spend the holiday.

What If Your Plan Doesn’t Mention Thanksgiving?

Some older or informal plans don’t mention Thanksgiving at all, or just say holidays will be shared “as the parties agree.” That works great until the parties don’t agree. If that’s you:

  • Try to agree, and put it in writing. Even a simple text confirming this year’s plan helps avoid last-minute surprises.
  • Consider mediation. A neutral mediator can often help parents settle on a holiday schedule without going to court.
  • Fix it for next year. If the holidays turn into a tug-of-war every year, it may be time to modify your parenting plan so the holiday schedule is spelled out.

One honest warning: if you file something with the court in mid-November, it’s unlikely to be decided before Thanksgiving, and Colorado state courts are closed on Thanksgiving Day. Planning ahead is your best friend here.

What If Your Co-Parent Doesn’t Follow the Schedule?

It’s incredibly frustrating when the other parent won’t hand over the kids, or keeps them hours past the agreed time. Take a breath, and try not to argue in front of your children. Instead:

  • Write down what happened: dates, times, and any messages.
  • Don’t get even. Don’t keep the kids from the other parent or hold back child support in return. Colorado treats child support and parenting time as separate issues, and getting even can backfire on you in court.
  • Know your options. Colorado has a specific process for parenting time problems. Once a parent files a motion, the other side has 21 days to respond to it and then the parent filing the motion has 7 days to reply. After that, the court will likely order mediation before setting a hearing or ruling on the pleadings.

If the court finds the schedule was violated, it can order things like makeup time, so a missed holiday can be replaced with holiday time. Generally, makeup time must happen within six months, or within a year if a holiday can’t be made up sooner. The court can also clarify or change the order, require a parenting class or counseling, order fines of up to $100 per incident, or order the other parent to pay your attorney fees and court costs.

If you believe your child is in danger, call 911 first. You can also ask the court to restrict the other parent’s time when a child faces imminent danger. Learn more about emergency custody in Colorado.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who gets the kids on Thanksgiving in Colorado?

It depends on your parenting plan. Colorado law doesn’t give Thanksgiving to either parent. Many plans alternate the holiday each year, split the day, or split the school break. If your plan is unclear, try to agree in writing and consider mediation.

Does the holiday schedule override the regular parenting schedule?

In most Colorado parenting plans, yes. The holiday schedule usually takes priority over the regular weekly schedule, but check the exact wording of your plan.

Can I take my child out of state for Thanksgiving?

Check your parenting plan for travel and notice rules. Even if your plan doesn’t require it, sharing your travel plans and contact information with the other parent helps avoid conflict.

What can I do if my ex keeps the kids on my Thanksgiving?

Write down what happened and avoid arguing in front of the children. You can ask the court for help under C.R.S. 14-10-129.5. If the court finds a violation, it can order makeup holiday time, fines, attorney fees, or other remedies.

Can we change the Thanksgiving schedule if we both agree?

Yes. For a one-time change, put your agreement in writing. For a lasting change, submit a written agreement to the court so it becomes part of your enforceable order.

Want a Calmer Thanksgiving This Year?

The holidays should be about your kids, not about who’s right. Then you can get back to the important things, like who gets the last slice of pie.
